title.text: Reviewing documents with AI

objects.text: How can AI help me review documents without missing what matters?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 5 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Today we review documents. Contracts, CVs and meeting notes pile up on an executive’s desk, and the risk is the clause nobody read. You will see what an AI assistant did with three real documents from our case company, compared with an answer key, and then you plan the review of a document of your own.

The question for today is this: How can AI help me review documents without missing what matters? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

slides.notes: Three parts matter most today. Ten minutes on the method, then thirty-five minutes on three cases with the results shown on slides, so nobody switches tools. After the break, forty-five minutes are yours, planning the review of a document from your own company. The last ten minutes are for deciding how much checking each kind of document gets.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  The readiness scorecard from Session 4 has six areas. Name as many as you can.
2.  Which area decides whether you may give a document to an AI tool at all?
3.  Why did your Session 4 inventory mark each source by sensitivity?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 4. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. The readiness scorecard from Session 4 has six areas. Name as many as you can. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Inventory, readable, complete and unique, metadata, rights and current. Each is scored green, amber or red.

Question two. Which area decides whether you may give a document to an AI tool at all? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Rights: who may use the information and for what, including personal and confidential data. A red on rights stops the project until someone who knows the rules has looked.

Question three. Why did your Session 4 inventory mark each source by sensitivity? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Because what you paste into a tool depends on how sensitive it is. Today’s CVs are personal data, so the same question applies.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Four words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Playbook. Your own rules for one kind of document, written as short numbered checks.

Source quote. The exact words in the document that support an issue. You can find them with the search function.

Flag. An issue the review raises. A flag without a quote is a draft to check.

Over-flagging. Raising an issue for text that already meets your rule.

title.text:
The method: give the AI your rules, ask
for quotes, check them, then decide

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_363cd973.png
objects.alt: The method: give the AI your rules, ask for quotes, check them, then decide

objects.text: AI can help with the first three steps. You own the fourth.

slides.notes:
This is the whole method, and today’s three cases all follow it. First you give the AI the document and your own rules. Second you ask it for the exact words behind every flag, which we call a source quote. Third you check: you search each quote in the document and see whether the words are there.

Fourth a person decides to accept, negotiate or escalate. AI can save you reading time in the first three steps. The fourth step stays with you, because you carry the responsibility and you know the business.

title.text:
Give the AI the document, your
rules and the table you want back

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_stack_7.70x4.80_8ef9cd66.png
objects.alt: Give the AI the document, your rules and the table you want back

objects.text: A review is only as good as the rules you give it.

runs.text: Allow the answer NOT FOUND.
Say: never invent a quote.
Share only what your policy allows.

slides.notes:
A review request has four layers. The document, which must be text you are allowed to share. Your rules, numbered, one per line, because without a rule an AI tool has nothing to compare with and will make up its own. The job, which is compare and quote.

And the format, a table with a quote in every row. Two details matter most. Allow the answer not found, so the tool is not pushed to invent something. And say never invent a quote. Remember the rights question from Session 4 before you paste anything.

title.text: The three requests we gave Claude, shortened

objects.text: Each request came with the full text of the document, and the review also had the playbook.
Agreement
Review the agreement against the playbook. List every clause that breaks it, with clause number, short exact quote, rule broken, why it matters and the change to ask for.
CVs
Rank the eight CVs for interview, strongest first. Two sentences of reasons each. List what to verify. Say who you would not shortlist and why.
Meeting notes
Turn these raw notes into decisions and action items with owner and due date. Use only the notes. Write “not stated” if missing.

slides.notes:
Here is what the assistant was asked, shortened. Three requests. For the agreement, I gave the full text of the Busoga Oils supply agreement and our review playbook with ten numbered rules. For the CVs, I gave the Dispatch Clerk job description and eight invented CVs. For the meeting, I gave a raw transcript of a Nile Valley Foods management meeting.

All documents and names are fictional. Each request went to Claude as a fresh session given only the prompt, told to use no other tool or file, and the answer keys were hidden. I cannot prove it used nothing else. Each request was run twice, in separate sessions, on the fourth of November 2026.

title.text:
Agreement review: both runs
found all three problem clauses

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_runs_11.90x4.25_06a85640.png

slides.notes:
This is Claude, in fresh sessions given only the prompt, on the fourth of November 2026, with the key hidden. Two runs. Both found all three deviations from the key: clause 3, the price change at sole discretion, clause 8, the ninety day notice against our thirty day maximum, and clause 10, the liability cap of three months of fees that also covers unsafe goods.

Neither flagged any of the seven clauses that comply. I searched every quote in the agreement text, and every one was there word for word. The key also mentions a diary date, about thirtieth of November 2026, which neither run gave, but the request did not ask for it.

One small slip: run one said the other nine clauses meet the playbook. Seven do, and clauses one and two have no rule.

objects.text: Layout of the Document Review Table template. The quotes are from the Busoga Oils agreement.

slides.notes:
Here is the layout of the Document Review Table template, with the three rows from the agreement. Each row has the clause, the exact words from the document, our rule, a risk level and a decision. The quote column is the one that matters. If you can search the document and find those words, the row is real.

If you cannot find them, do not rely on the row. In the full template there are also columns for the owner and the next step. A person fills in the decision column, and the liability row goes to the Managing Director and a lawyer.

title.text:
Check every quote: search it, match
the words, then trust the row

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_5452eb82.png
objects.alt: Check every quote: search it, match the words, then trust the row

objects.text: In these two runs every quote was found. Another run can paraphrase a clause or invent one.

slides.notes:
The check takes about ten seconds a row. Copy the quote, search for it in the document, and compare the words and the numbers. If the words are not there, fix the row or delete it. In our two runs every quote was found, but that is no promise about the next run, the next document or another product.

A fluent answer with a wrong quote is the dangerous one, because it looks checked. So the rule in your company is simple: no quote that you can find, no flag that you rely on.

title.text:
CV shortlist: both runs ranked the strong
CVs high and caught the inflated one

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_runs_11.90x4.25_a4e90a57.png
objects.alt: CV shortlist: both runs ranked the strong CVs high and caught the inflated one

objects.text: Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden, 2 runs. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
This is Claude, fresh sessions given only the prompt, fourth of November 2026, key hidden, two runs, and the key is a guide with several reasonable answers and no strict ranking. It lists Tumusiime, Wandera, Avako, Apio and Lomuria. Both runs put Tumusiime first and Avako second, with Wandera third or fourth.

They differ on the others. Run 1 left the candidate with the career gap off its suggested shortlist, while Run 2 shortlisted that candidate. Both treated the candidate with an unchecked Kenyan diploma as a shortlist with a check. Both refused to shortlist the CV with the inflated claims, where the key says verify first. Gold shows where a run differs from the key’s guide.

title.text:
CV traps: the career gap, the foreign
diploma, the inflated claims and bias

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_runs_11.90x4.25_dcbd547c.png
objects.alt: CV traps: the career gap, the foreign diploma, the inflated claims and bias

objects.text: Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden, 2 runs. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
Four traps in the CVs. The career gap: both runs wrote that it should not count against the candidate, but Run 1 still ranked that candidate sixth, off its shortlist. The foreign diploma: both flagged it for checking. The inflated claims: both caught the ten years, the fleet of two hundred, one hundred and fifty staff and the four hundred percent, with no referees.

Names: the stated reasons of neither run mention names, and both added a fairness note unprompted. Both said do not rank on home area and then used it, for example based in Tororo, relocation needed. The job is in Jinja, so distance is job relevant, but the notes should say so.

We cannot see what else shaped the ranking. I also recomputed years: Run 1 counted two years for 2023 to present, where the dates say about three.

title.text:
A person decides who is interviewed,
because bias can hide in a fluent reason

objects.text: Sensible reasons are not proof that a ranking is fair.

objects.text: Remove names and home areas. Score job facts.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.70.png

objects.text: Keep the career gap for the interview.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_lock_0.70.png

objects.text: A CV is personal data: the 2019 Act applies.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_stamp_0.70.png

objects.text: Equal-treatment rules may apply: ask your lawyer.

slides.notes:
So why does a person decide?

A fluent reason is not proof that a ranking is fair. A tool can repeat bias from its training without saying so, and you may not see it. Safer habits: remove names, photos and home areas and score only job facts, keep the career gap for the interview and out of the score, and record who decided and why.

A CV is personal data, and in Uganda the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 applies. My understanding is that employment equal-treatment rules may apply too, and the EU AI Act classes recruitment tools as high risk, so check the current text and confirm with your lawyer. Session 9 covers this.

Here is the summary for all three cases. For an agreement, AI can find the clauses, quote them and propose changes, and a person checks the quotes, decides whether to accept, negotiate or escalate, and signs. For CVs, AI can pull out facts and flag gaps to verify, and a person chooses who is interviewed and why.

For meeting notes, AI can list decisions, actions, owners and dates, and a person confirms each one is real and sends the list. For every one of them, a person owns the result and records who decided.

Practice: choose one document
you review and write its rules

Your own company task
Pick one kind of document you review in your own company.

Write five to ten rules, one line each, numbered.
Put the number, date or period in each rule.
Mark any rule you cannot state clearly.

objects.text: You keep: A numbered rule list, one line for each rule.

slides.notes:
Take fifteen minutes. Choose one kind of document that you review often in your own company. A supplier quote, a contract, a policy, a CV pack. Write five to ten rules for it, numbered, one line each. Put the number in the rule: thirty days, five percent, twelve months.

If a rule is vague, such as a reasonable price, write it anyway and mark it, because the vague rules are the ones where a person must decide. This is a writing exercise on paper. You do not run anything today.

title.text:
Practice: write the request and
say what the AI may not decide

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own company task
Write the request you would give an AI assistant for this document.

runs.text: Name the document and say what you will paste, and what you will remove first.
Add your numbered rules.
Ask for a table: clause, exact quote, rule, reason, change.
Add: NOT FOUND if missing, never invent a quote.
Write one decision the AI may never make.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_0dc15d8c.png

objects.text: You keep: A request you could paste into an assistant, and one decision kept for you.

slides.notes:
Another fifteen minutes. Write the request you would give an assistant, on paper. Say which document it is and what you will remove first, such as names and personal data. Add your numbered rules. Ask for a table with the clause, the exact quote, the rule, the reason and the change.

Allow the answer not found and say never invent a quote. Finally, write one decision the assistant may never make for you.

title.text: Practice: plan the checks, with names and a time

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own company task
Write who checks the result and when, for your document.

runs.text: Name the person who searches every quote.
Name the person who decides: accept, negotiate or escalate.
Write what must be removed before you share the document.
Choose how you record who decided, and when.

objects.text: You keep: A one page check plan with named people.

slides.notes:
The last fifteen minutes of your own work. Plan the checks, with names and a time. Who searches every quote, and how soon?

Who decides to accept, negotiate or escalate, and who do they escalate to?

What do you remove from the document before it goes anywhere?

And where do you record who decided, so that you can answer later. In my example, Joseph Mugisha searches the quotes the same day and the Managing Director decides on the liability row. When you finish, read your plan aloud to the group.

objects.text: No AI at all
The document may not be shared with any tool.
Record the level and one reason on your check plan.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. How much checking does your document get?

Read it all yourself, for high stakes or personal data. An AI draft with every quote checked, which suits contracts and quotes. An AI draft with a spot check, which suits low stakes work such as meeting notes, with the person who chaired the meeting confirming the list.

Or no AI at all, if the document may not be shared with any tool. Say your choice and your reason aloud, and write them on the plan. You can change the level later as you gain evidence.
